framework_name: UNESCO Guidance for AI in Education & Research
framework_source: UNESCO (2023). Guidance for generative AI in education and research. UNESDOC pf0000386693. ISBN 978-92-3-100612-8.
reasonlens_implementation_note: This file operationalises the UNESCO Guidance document for the ReasonLens platform as an institutional policy maturity assessment. The original UNESCO document is structured as regulatory guidance with policy measures and stakeholder frameworks, not as a maturity model. ReasonLens imposes a 4-dimension x 3-level maturity structure to enable comparable assessment alongside other institutional frameworks (THE DMI, QS AI Capability, JISC AI Maturity). The four dimensions synthesise UNESCO's eight policy action areas and four-stakeholder regulatory framework into assessable institutional governance dimensions. The three levels (Emerging/Developing/Established) are a ReasonLens construct informed by the JISC AI Maturity Model's stage-based approach.

dimensions.name: Human-Centred AI
dimensions.description: The extent to which the institution ensures that AI deployment protects human agency, supports human decision-making, and centres educational relationships on human needs, values, and rights. Covers governance of AI-human interaction, protection of learner and staff autonomy, and human oversight mechanisms.

dimensions.name: Safe & Equitable
dimensions.description: The extent to which the institution implements mechanisms to ensure AI systems are safe, secure, inclusive, and equitable. Covers risk assessment, bias auditing, accessibility, digital divide mitigation, and protection of vulnerable populations including age-appropriate use.

dimensions.name: Ethics & Accountability
dimensions.description: The extent to which the institution establishes ethical governance structures, accountability mechanisms, and regulatory compliance for AI use. Covers ethics committees, data protection, transparency requirements, AI use policies, academic integrity frameworks, and accountability chains.

dimensions.name: Evidence-Based
dimensions.description: The extent to which the institution builds and uses evidence to inform AI adoption decisions, evaluates AI effectiveness through rigorous methods, and contributes to the broader knowledge base. Covers pilot evaluation, impact assessment, research partnerships, and evidence-informed policy development.

levels.name: Emerging
levels.description: The institution recognises AI as relevant to education and research and has begun initial responses, but lacks coordinated policy, systematic governance, or evidence-based deployment. AI use is happening informally, and institutional responses are reactive or ad hoc.

levels.name: Developing
levels.description: The institution has established initial policies, governance structures, and evaluation mechanisms for AI in education and research. Formal initiatives are underway but not yet comprehensive, institution-wide, or fully embedded in standard practice.

levels.name: Established
levels.description: The institution has comprehensive, embedded, and actively maintained AI governance, with evidence-driven policy, systematic safety and equity mechanisms, and continuous improvement processes. AI governance is integrated into institutional strategy and decision-making structures.

data.rationale: Human-Centred AI governance maps to THE DMI Planning & Governance: Strategy, as both address how the institution governs technology deployment at the strategic level.
data.what_transfers: Both frameworks assess institutional maturity. THE DMI provides the broader digital maturity context within which AI governance sits. Institutions with higher DMI maturity in governance and data are better positioned for AI governance.
data.what_does_not_transfer: THE DMI is technology-agnostic (all digital technology). UNESCO Guidance is AI-specific. DMI does not address AI-specific ethical, safety, or human agency concerns. DMI maturity levels (Incidental/Intentional/Integrated/Optimised) do not map neatly to UNESCO Guidance levels (Emerging/Developing/Established).

data.rationale: Human-Centred AI maps to QS AI Capability governance dimensions, both addressing institutional governance of AI deployment.
data.what_transfers: Both frameworks assess institutional AI capability at the institutional level. QS focuses on competitive positioning and capability development; UNESCO Guidance focuses on ethical and responsible deployment. Together they provide a more complete picture.
data.what_does_not_transfer: QS is competitive and benchmarking-oriented. UNESCO Guidance is normative and rights-based. Different philosophical foundations and different primary audiences (institutional leaders vs. policymakers).

data.rationale: Human-Centred AI maps to JISC Strategic Adoption of AI, as both address institutional governance decisions about AI deployment.
data.what_transfers: JISC is the closest structural peer: UK HE/FE focused, AI-specific, with maturity stages. JISC stages (Not Yet Started/Approaching/Experimenting/Operational/Embedded) provide a more granular progression than UNESCO Guidance's three levels. Thematic alignment is strong, especially around safe and responsible use.
data.what_does_not_transfer: JISC is UK-specific with UK regulatory assumptions. UNESCO Guidance is global. JISC includes teaching/learning and professional services dimensions that UNESCO Guidance does not. UNESCO Guidance has stronger emphasis on human agency and evidence-building.

data.target_framework: UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Students (ReasonLens: sc-*)
data.rationale: Institutional human-centred governance creates the conditions for student AI understanding by ensuring AI tools used in education maintain human agency and are transparent.
data.what_transfers: Institutional policy creates the environment for student competency development. UNESCO explicitly links the Guidance document to the competency frameworks, particularly through policy measure 4 (develop AI competencies for learners). The policy-competency link is bidirectional: ethically competent students contribute to institutional ethical culture.
data.what_does_not_transfer: Different unit of analysis (institution vs. individual). Different evidence types (institutional documents vs. student behaviours). Different respondent profiles (institutional leaders vs. students). The institutional framework cannot assess individual competency and vice versa.

data.target_framework: UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Teachers
data.rationale: Institutional ethics governance connects to teacher ethics competency. Teachers implement institutional ethics policies and develop student ethical competency.
data.what_transfers: The Guidance document explicitly calls for building teacher capacity (policy measure 5). Teacher competency is both an enabler and an outcome of institutional policy. Teachers are the primary implementers of AI governance in educational contexts.
data.what_does_not_transfer: Different unit of analysis. Teachers implement policy but do not set it. Institutional governance operates at a different level than individual teacher competency.

data.rationale: ISTE Standards for Students do not address institutional governance. ISTE's focus on individual student competency has no equivalent for institutional human-centred AI governance.
